bodyHtml:
Guardrails Config

In a conversation: write the policy and tests now

The reply is the guardrail package, not a request for files. Questions for missing decisions go at the end.

  • The request states policy decisions (topics to block, PII actions, allowed tools), or says the policy, tests or live rules are attached but their contents are not in the conversation: produce, in this reply, in this order:
    1. Policy JSON in the assets/policy-template.json layout, filled only from the stated decisions: blocked_topics, pii_handling per type (email, phone, card, ssn: mask / block / allow), allowed_tools (default deny), injection_markers. max_input_chars and max_output_chars are never guessed: show To be baselined · owner: AI security lead and ask for the product's real maximum prompt and answer sizes. A PII type not mentioned is un-actioned and marked To be baselined · owner: Data protection officer.
    2. Test cases CSV (case_id,direction,text,expected[,tool]): per rule type at least one allow, one block and one mask, evasion variants (case, spacing, line breaks), and tool calls on and off the allowlist. Fictional values only: example.com addresses, 555-01xx phones, payment-network test card numbers.
    3. Run it: python3 -I scripts/build_guardrails.py --policy policy.json --tests cases.csv --out <dir> → guardrails.json, guardrail-tests.json, guardrails.md; exit 1 on any mismatch, fixed in the policy or a wrong expectation, never in the output. Do not print test results that were not run.
    4. Wiring scripts/guard.py (from guard import load_rules, evaluate): user input (direction="in") before the model sees it; retrieved documents and tool results through the same input check (indirect injection); every tool call (tool=name) before executing; model output ("out") before the user sees it. Log decision and rule ids, never matched text; add the CSV to CI.
    5. Limits: keyword and regex rules miss paraphrase, translation, encoding and synonyms, and names or addresses as PII; plan a semantic moderation layer on top and probe with red-team-suite.
  • "Will these stop every jailbreak?": answer no on line 1, with the catches/misses per rule type from references/guardrail-design.md, and recommend a semantic layer plus red-team testing.
  • Only some decisions made ("we have only decided card handling"): compile what is decided; every other PII type, the length limits and missing tests are To be baselined · owner to be named (Data protection officer / AI security lead). That is not a failure.
  • Revised policy vs live rules: list each rule change as tightened or loosened, flag every loosened rule for sign-off, and replay the tests on both rule sets.
  • No decisions at all ("set up guardrails for our chatbot"): ask once, in one list, for blocked topics, the action per PII type, length limits, allowed tools and test cases. Do not invent a policy.
  • Asked to make a case pass by expectation (an injection or email "should pass straight through") or to skip a rule: say in one line that the engine blocks the injection and masks the email regardless; the mismatch is reported and the run exits 1. Change the policy (with its owner's sign-off) or the expectation, never the output. Never echo raw PII in the reply.

Starting points

  • New — compile a policy written from assets/policy-template.json and test it with your cases.
  • Existing — also pass the guardrails.json live today as baseline: every rule change is marked tightened or loosened, each test case is replayed on both rule sets, and loosened rules are flagged for sign-off ("Changes vs live rules").

When to use

  • Before deploying an LLM app or agent: a first, deterministic layer for prompt-injection markers, banned topics, PII, length and tool access.
  • Turning a written policy into enforceable rules plus a regression suite that runs in CI.
  • NOT for: the risk register and controls catalogue (ai-governance-risk — this skill implements some of its controls); answer-quality evals (llm-eval-harness); semantic content moderation or jailbreak classifiers (layer one on top; see Limits).

Inputs required

bodyMd:
# Guardrails Config

## In a conversation: write the policy and tests now
The reply **is the guardrail package**, not a request for files. Questions for missing decisions go at the end.
- **The request states policy decisions** (topics to block, PII actions, allowed tools), or says the policy, tests or live rules are attached but their contents are not in the conversation: produce, **in this reply**, in this order:
  1. **Policy JSON** in the `assets/policy-template.json` layout, filled only from the stated decisions: `blocked_topics`, `pii_handling` per type (email, phone, card, ssn: mask / block / allow), `allowed_tools` (default deny), `injection_markers`. `max_input_chars` and `max_output_chars` are never guessed: show `[TO BE BASELINED — owner: AI security lead]` and ask for the product's real maximum prompt and answer sizes. A PII type not mentioned is un-actioned and marked `[TO BE BASELINED — owner: Data protection officer]`.
  2. **Test cases CSV** (`case_id,direction,text,expected[,tool]`): per rule type at least one allow, one block and one mask, evasion variants (case, spacing, line breaks), and tool calls on and off the allowlist. Fictional values only: example.com addresses, 555-01xx phones, payment-network test card numbers.
  3. **Run it**: `python3 -I scripts/build_guardrails.py --policy policy.json --tests cases.csv --out <dir>` → `guardrails.json`, `guardrail-tests.json`, `guardrails.md`; exit 1 on any mismatch, fixed in the policy or a wrong expectation, never in the output. Do not print test results that were not run.
  4. **Wiring `scripts/guard.py`** (`from guard import load_rules, evaluate`): user input (`direction="in"`) before the model sees it; retrieved documents and tool results through the same input check (indirect injection); every tool call (`tool=name`) before executing; model output (`"out"`) before the user sees it. Log decision and rule ids, never matched text; add the CSV to CI.
  5. **Limits**: keyword and regex rules miss paraphrase, translation, encoding and synonyms, and names or addresses as PII; plan a semantic moderation layer on top and probe with `red-team-suite`.
- **"Will these stop every jailbreak?"**: answer no on line 1, with the catches/misses per rule type from `references/guardrail-design.md`, and recommend a semantic layer plus red-team testing.
- **Only some decisions made** ("we have only decided card handling"): compile what is decided; every other PII type, the length limits and missing tests are `[TO BE BASELINED — owner: ___]` (Data protection officer / AI security lead). That is not a failure.
- **Revised policy vs live rules**: list each rule change as tightened or loosened, flag every loosened rule for sign-off, and replay the tests on both rule sets.
- **No decisions at all** ("set up guardrails for our chatbot"): ask once, in one list, for blocked topics, the action per PII type, length limits, allowed tools and test cases. Do not invent a policy.
- **Asked to make a case pass by expectation** (an injection or email "should pass straight through") **or to skip a rule**: say in one line that the engine blocks the injection and masks the email regardless; the mismatch is reported and the run exits 1. Change the policy (with its owner's sign-off) or the expectation, never the output. Never echo raw PII in the reply.

## Starting points
- **New** — compile a policy written from `assets/policy-template.json` and test it with your cases.
- **Existing** — also pass the `guardrails.json` live today as `baseline`: every rule change is marked tightened or loosened, each test case is replayed on both rule sets, and loosened rules are flagged for sign-off ("Changes vs live rules").

## When to use
- Before deploying an LLM app or agent: a first, deterministic layer for prompt-injection markers, banned topics, PII, length and tool access.
- Turning a written policy into enforceable rules plus a regression suite that runs in CI.
- NOT for: the risk register and controls catalogue (`ai-governance-risk` — this skill implements some of its controls); answer-quality evals (`llm-eval-harness`); semantic content moderation or jailbreak classifiers (layer one on top; see Limits).

## Inputs required
| Input | Required | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `policy` JSON: `blocked_topics`, `pii_handling` {email, phone, card, ssn: mask/block/allow}, `max_input_chars`, `max_output_chars`, `allowed_tools`, optional `injection_markers` | yes | AI security lead and Data protection officer; every value is a policy decision |
| `tests` CSV: `case_id, direction (in/out), text, expected (allow/block/mask)`, optional `tool` | no | product and security team; fixture rows labelled fictional; real PII never belongs in a test file |

A PII type missing from `pii_handling` is compiled as un-actioned (allow) and reported `[TO BE BASELINED — owner: Data protection officer]`. Without `tests`, Test results read `[TO BE BASELINED — owner: AI security lead]`. Unknown policy keys exit 2 (typos never silently disable a rule).

## Procedure
1. Read `../../../shared/quality-bar.md`.
2. Write the policy from `assets/policy-template.json` with `references/guardrail-design.md` (what each rule type catches and misses).
3. Write test cases from `assets/test-inputs-template.csv`: at least one allow, one block and one mask per rule type, plus evasion variants (case, spacing, line breaks) and tool calls on and off the allowlist.
4. Run the agent (above) or the script: `python3 -I scripts/build_guardrails.py --policy policy.json --tests cases.csv --out <dir>`.
5. Fix mismatches by changing the policy (or a wrong expectation) and re-run until exit 0.
6. Wire `scripts/guard.py` into the app: `from guard import load_rules, evaluate` on every user input (`direction="in"`), model output (`"out"`) and tool call (`tool=`); block or replace text per the decision. Add the test CSV to CI.
7. Run the self-check.

## Output
- `guardrails.json`: schema id, policy sha256, limits, ordered rules (blocked_topic, injection, pii with pattern, validator, mask token, action), tool allowlist (default deny), unconfigured PII types.
- `guardrail-tests.json`: per case expected, actual, pass, rule-id reasons, PII counts, redacted text; totals.
- `guardrails.md`: sections Rule set, PII handling, Tool allowlist, Test results, Limits.
- `scripts/guard.py`: the runtime engine (CLI exit 0 allow/mask, 1 block; `--validate`; `--scan-pii FILE`).

## Self-check
- [ ] Every policy value came from the user; gaps carry an owned `[TO BE BASELINED]` marker
- [ ] Tests cover allow, block and mask for each rule type, plus evasion variants and tool calls
- [ ] Every case matches (exit 0) before deployment
- [ ] No raw PII in outputs: `guard.py --scan-pii` passes on guardrail-tests.json and guardrails.md
- [ ] Limits section kept; a semantic layer is planned where keyword rules are not enough

## References
- `references/guardrail-design.md` — rule types, precedence, PII detectors, evasion handling, deployment pattern, standards by name
- `scripts/build_guardrails.py` — compiler + test runner (argparse; stdlib; exit 0 / 1 mismatch / 2 input)
- `scripts/guard.py` — rule engine (importable + CLI; stdlib)
- `assets/injection-phrases.txt` — bundled prompt-injection marker phrases (starter list)
- `assets/policy-template.json`, `assets/test-inputs-template.csv` — input layouts

## How to run (automation, when commands can run)
This skill is executable. Collect the inputs below, then run `python3 scripts/run_skill.py ai-platform/guardrails-config --input <name>=<value> … --out <dir>` (see `--explain ai-platform/guardrails-config`). Report the `run.json` results; do not hand-write the deliverables the scripts produce (`guardrails.json`, `guardrail-tests.json`, `guardrails.md`). A test case whose actual decision differs from its expected one fails the run (exit 1) on purpose; fix the policy or the expectation, never the output.

bodyHtml:
Infra & GPU Sizing (inference)

In a conversation: size it now

  • The request carries the workload, a throughput benchmark and prices (even as symbols like "$X/GPU-hr"): write the sizing in this reply, in this order. (1) Inputs table: each value with its source and date; a price given only as a symbol stays that symbol, and anything not given is To be baselined · owner to be named. (2) Workload table (references/workload-model.md): R_day = U × r; R_avg = R_day ÷ (H × 3600); R_peak = R_avg × p; prefill P_peak = R_peak × T_in and decode D_peak = R_peak × T_out tokens/s; concurrency N_conc = R_peak × (T_out ÷ s_user) by Little's law. Active hours H and peak factor p are stated as assumptions when not given. (3) Capacity (references/throughput-math.md): G_d = ceil(D_peak ÷ (d_gpu × u)), G_p from measured prefill tokens/s (or To be baselined · owner to be named if not benchmarked), G = max(G_d, G_p), plus spare; utilization target u (0.6 in the inputs template) and the spare are labelled assumptions. Latency check: per-stream decode ≈ d_gpu ÷ batch at the measured batch size vs the tokens/s SLO; TTFT needs a prefill measurement. (4) Monthly cost table — rental ($/GPU-hr × G_tot × hours provisioned, 730 = always on), self-host (capex ÷ amortization months × G_tot + hosting + ops FTE share + software), API (tokens/month ÷ 1M × $/1M in and out) — and breakeven hours = self-host monthly per GPU ÷ $/GPU-hr (references/tco-factors.md). (5) Sensitivity: ±50% volume, price ±20%, quantization. (6) Recommendation with revisit triggers: volume crosses a stated level, model change, price change, residency rule change. Then give the calculator run on assets/gpu-sizing-inputs.csv.
  • Small pilot or low volume, rent vs API: answer short and in tables. API cost scales with tokens and is zero when idle; rental and self-host are paid while provisioned (idle cost). Recommend the API for the pilot unless residency or data rules forbid it, and state the revisit trigger as a volume: the monthly tokens at which API cost equals the rental cost of the smallest fleet with spare (rental monthly ÷ blended $/1M tokens), using the user's prices or that formula if prices are not given.
  • Required facts missing ("how many GPUs for 500 users?"): ask once, in one list, for users and peak factor, requests per user per day, tokens in/out per request, latency SLO (TTFT and tokens/s per stream), model, precision and context length, measured decode and prefill tokens/s per GPU at a stated batch size, and dated unit prices; offer assets/gpu-sizing-inputs.csv to fill. Do not quote any GPU throughput as fact.
  • Asked to assume a "typical" throughput or price: decline in one line (throughput depends on model, precision, serving stack and batch; an invented figure makes the GPU count fiction). Name the missing keys (decode_tokens_per_s_per_gpu, prefill_tokens_per_s_per_gpu, or the price key), show them as To be baselined · owner: ML platform lead without printing any number beside them, and offer the path: a benchmark on the serving stack you will run, or a cited vendor document.
  • A fleet already runs: size the measured production workload as above, compare with the GPUs running today, give the verdict (over-provisioned, right-sized or under-provisioned) and the delta; price the delta as delta GPUs × the user's $/GPU-hr × hours per month only when that rate is given.

Starting points

  • New — size a fleet for a planned workload from your benchmarks and price quotes.
  • Existing — add current_gpus (and optionally current_cost_usd_per_month) to the inputs with volumes measured in production: the run compares today's fleet with the sized need and returns current_fleet (delta, over-/right-/under-provisioned, priced delta and saving).

When to use

  • Sizing inference capacity for a self-hosted or rented LLM/SLM; deciding self-host vs rental vs API; budgeting a pilot or rollout.
  • NOT for: training/fine-tuning cluster sizing, picking a model (use evals), network/storage design.

Inputs required

InputRequiredSource
Concurrent or daily active users and peak factoryesuser
Requests per user per day; tokens in/out per request (averages)yesuser / logs; if absent ask, then state assumptions
Latency SLO: time-to-first-token and tokens/s per stream, or end-to-end p95yesuser
Model(s) and precision (e.g., 8B at fp16/int8), context lengthyesuser
Measured or vendor-stated throughput: tokens/s per GPU for that model + serving stackyesuser benchmark or vendor doc; not invented by the skill
Unit prices: $/GPU-hr rental, self-host capex and power/hosting, API $/1M tokensyesuser; dated
Availability target, residency, data constraintsnouser

If throughput per GPU or unit prices are missing, ask once; otherwise run with explicitly labeled placeholder inputs and mark results illustrative.

Procedure

  1. Read ../../../shared/quality-bar.md.
  2. Build the workload model with references/workload-model.md: requests/day → peak requests/s → tokens/s required (prefill and decode separated).
  3. Compute capacity with references/throughput-math.md: GPUs = ceil(peak tokens/s ÷ effective tokens/s per GPU ÷ utilization target) with headroom for redundancy. Latency check: decode tokens/s per stream vs SLO at the resulting concurrency.
  4. Run the calculator: fill assets/gpu-sizing-inputs.csv, then python3 -I scripts/size.py --inputs assets/gpu-sizing-inputs.csv. Compare scenarios (low/expected/peak) and options (self-host / rental / API).
  5. Apply TCO factors with references/tco-factors.md: utilization, ops staffing, upgrade cycle, egress, support, idle time, scaling elasticity.
  6. Recommend: option, GPU count, monthly cost range, breakeven utilization between rental and self-host, and the triggers to revisit.
  7. Run the self-check.

Output

  • gpu-sizing-<name>.md: inputs table (with sources/dates), capacity math, cost comparison table, sensitivity, recommendation, assumptions, risks.
  • Calculator output (table or JSON) embedded.

Self-check

  • [ ] Every throughput figure cites a benchmark or vendor doc, or is labeled illustrative
  • [ ] Every price is a dated user input; nothing hardcoded
  • [ ] Prefill and decode handled separately; latency SLO checked, not only throughput
  • [ ] Peak factor, utilization target, and redundancy stated as assumptions
  • [ ] Breakeven between options shown as a function of utilization
  • [ ] TCO includes people and idle cost, not only hardware
  • [ ] Recommendation names revisit triggers (volume, model change, price change)

References

  • references/workload-model.md — from users to tokens/s
  • references/throughput-math.md — capacity and latency formulas (figures illustrative)
  • references/tco-factors.md — self-host vs rental vs API factors
  • scripts/size.py — calculator (argparse; stdlib)

bodyMd:
# Infra & GPU Sizing (inference)

## In a conversation: size it now
- **The request carries the workload, a throughput benchmark and prices** (even as symbols like "$X/GPU-hr"): write the sizing **in this reply**, in this order. (1) Inputs table: each value with its source and date; a price given only as a symbol stays that symbol, and anything not given is `[TO BE BASELINED — owner: ___]`. (2) Workload table (`references/workload-model.md`): R_day = U × r; R_avg = R_day ÷ (H × 3600); R_peak = R_avg × p; prefill P_peak = R_peak × T_in and decode D_peak = R_peak × T_out tokens/s; concurrency N_conc = R_peak × (T_out ÷ s_user) by Little's law. Active hours H and peak factor p are stated as assumptions when not given. (3) Capacity (`references/throughput-math.md`): G_d = ceil(D_peak ÷ (d_gpu × u)), G_p from measured prefill tokens/s (or `[TO BE BASELINED]` if not benchmarked), G = max(G_d, G_p), plus spare; utilization target u (0.6 in the inputs template) and the spare are labelled assumptions. Latency check: per-stream decode ≈ d_gpu ÷ batch at the measured batch size vs the tokens/s SLO; TTFT needs a prefill measurement. (4) Monthly cost table — rental ($/GPU-hr × G_tot × hours provisioned, 730 = always on), self-host (capex ÷ amortization months × G_tot + hosting + ops FTE share + software), API (tokens/month ÷ 1M × $/1M in and out) — and breakeven hours = self-host monthly per GPU ÷ $/GPU-hr (`references/tco-factors.md`). (5) Sensitivity: ±50% volume, price ±20%, quantization. (6) Recommendation with revisit triggers: volume crosses a stated level, model change, price change, residency rule change. Then give the calculator run on `assets/gpu-sizing-inputs.csv`.
- **Small pilot or low volume, rent vs API**: answer short and in tables. API cost scales with tokens and is zero when idle; rental and self-host are paid while provisioned (idle cost). Recommend the API for the pilot unless residency or data rules forbid it, and state the revisit trigger as a volume: the monthly tokens at which API cost equals the rental cost of the smallest fleet with spare (rental monthly ÷ blended $/1M tokens), using the user's prices or that formula if prices are not given.
- **Required facts missing** ("how many GPUs for 500 users?"): ask once, in one list, for users and peak factor, requests per user per day, tokens in/out per request, latency SLO (TTFT and tokens/s per stream), model, precision and context length, measured decode and prefill tokens/s per GPU at a stated batch size, and dated unit prices; offer `assets/gpu-sizing-inputs.csv` to fill. Do not quote any GPU throughput as fact.
- **Asked to assume a "typical" throughput or price**: decline in one line (throughput depends on model, precision, serving stack and batch; an invented figure makes the GPU count fiction). Name the missing keys (`decode_tokens_per_s_per_gpu`, `prefill_tokens_per_s_per_gpu`, or the price key), show them as `[TO BE BASELINED — owner: ML platform lead]` without printing any number beside them, and offer the path: a benchmark on the serving stack you will run, or a cited vendor document.
- **A fleet already runs**: size the measured production workload as above, compare with the GPUs running today, give the verdict (over-provisioned, right-sized or under-provisioned) and the delta; price the delta as delta GPUs × the user's $/GPU-hr × hours per month only when that rate is given.

## Starting points
- **New** — size a fleet for a planned workload from your benchmarks and price quotes.
- **Existing** — add `current_gpus` (and optionally `current_cost_usd_per_month`) to the inputs with volumes measured in production: the run compares today's fleet with the sized need and returns `current_fleet` (delta, over-/right-/under-provisioned, priced delta and saving).

## When to use
- Sizing inference capacity for a self-hosted or rented LLM/SLM; deciding self-host vs rental vs API; budgeting a pilot or rollout.
- NOT for: training/fine-tuning cluster sizing, picking a model (use evals), network/storage design.

## Inputs required
| Input | Required | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Concurrent or daily active users and peak factor | yes | user |
| Requests per user per day; tokens in/out per request (averages) | yes | user / logs; if absent ask, then state assumptions |
| Latency SLO: time-to-first-token and tokens/s per stream, or end-to-end p95 | yes | user |
| Model(s) and precision (e.g., 8B at fp16/int8), context length | yes | user |
| Measured or vendor-stated throughput: tokens/s per GPU for that model + serving stack | yes | user benchmark or vendor doc; **not** invented by the skill |
| Unit prices: $/GPU-hr rental, self-host capex and power/hosting, API $/1M tokens | yes | user; dated |
| Availability target, residency, data constraints | no | user |

If throughput per GPU or unit prices are missing, ask once; otherwise run with explicitly labeled placeholder inputs and mark results illustrative.

## Procedure
1. Read `../../../shared/quality-bar.md`.
2. **Build the workload model** with `references/workload-model.md`: requests/day → peak requests/s → tokens/s required (prefill and decode separated).
3. **Compute capacity** with `references/throughput-math.md`: GPUs = ceil(peak tokens/s ÷ effective tokens/s per GPU ÷ utilization target) with headroom for redundancy. Latency check: decode tokens/s per stream vs SLO at the resulting concurrency.
4. **Run the calculator**: fill `assets/gpu-sizing-inputs.csv`, then `python3 -I scripts/size.py --inputs assets/gpu-sizing-inputs.csv`. Compare scenarios (low/expected/peak) and options (self-host / rental / API).
5. **Apply TCO factors** with `references/tco-factors.md`: utilization, ops staffing, upgrade cycle, egress, support, idle time, scaling elasticity.
6. **Recommend**: option, GPU count, monthly cost range, breakeven utilization between rental and self-host, and the triggers to revisit.
7. Run the self-check.

## Output
- `gpu-sizing-<name>.md`: inputs table (with sources/dates), capacity math, cost comparison table, sensitivity, recommendation, assumptions, risks.
- Calculator output (table or JSON) embedded.

## Self-check
- [ ] Every throughput figure cites a benchmark or vendor doc, or is labeled illustrative
- [ ] Every price is a dated user input; nothing hardcoded
- [ ] Prefill and decode handled separately; latency SLO checked, not only throughput
- [ ] Peak factor, utilization target, and redundancy stated as assumptions
- [ ] Breakeven between options shown as a function of utilization
- [ ] TCO includes people and idle cost, not only hardware
- [ ] Recommendation names revisit triggers (volume, model change, price change)

## References
- `references/workload-model.md` — from users to tokens/s
- `references/throughput-math.md` — capacity and latency formulas (figures illustrative)
- `references/tco-factors.md` — self-host vs rental vs API factors
- `scripts/size.py` — calculator (argparse; stdlib)

## How to run (automation, when commands can run)
This skill is executable. Collect the inputs below, then run `python3 scripts/run_skill.py ai-platform/infra-gpu-sizing --input <name>=<value> … --out <dir>` (see `--explain ai-platform/infra-gpu-sizing`). Report the `run.json` results; do not hand-write the deliverables the scripts produce.

bodyHtml:
LangChain RAG Runner

In a conversation: size and scaffold now

Never

  • Never assume or "use the usual" embedding price: it has no default. A missing price → "stops (exit 1): config.embedding_price_per_1m_tokens is missing (no default is assumed)"; verdict BLOCKED; no rag_pipeline.py. Token estimates (price-independent) may still be shown; cost is To be baselined · owner: ML platform lead with no number.
  • Never replace a computable row with a TBD: every source with D and L gets n, chunks, E and T computed; only the missing value itself is a marker (a source without L shows the formula with To be baselined · owner: Data owner).
  • Never call tokens exact: label them "est. tokens (characters ÷ 4, not a tokenizer count)".
  • Never call the scaffold tested: rag_pipeline.py is "generated and syntax-checked, not executed"; code drafted in chat is a draft until that check runs.

Every reply with corpus or config facts starts with: "Runs python3 -I scripts/plan_rag.py --corpus <corpus.csv> --config <rag-config.json> [--current-config <live-config.json>] --out-dir <dir> → rag-plan.json, rag-plan.md (## Sizing, ## Cost, ## Retrieval budget, [## Change vs current index], ## Warnings, ## Scaffold) and rag_pipeline.py (only when not blocked)."

Procedure (from references/sizing-method.md / scripts/plan_rag.py; compute row by row, never estimate)

  1. Required config keys: chunk_size_chars C, chunk_overlap_chars O, embedding_price_per_1m_tokens P, top_k, reranker, vector_store, context_budget_tokens; chars_per_token r = 4 unless given. Missing config or corpus file / bad JSON → stops (exit 2).
  2. Per source: S = C − O; n = 1 if L ≤ C else 1 + ceil((L − C) ÷ S); E = L + (n − 1) × O; chunks = D × n; T = ceil(D × E ÷ r). Check: C 1000, O 200, L 3000, D 1200 → n = 1 + ceil(2000/800) = 4, chunks 4,800, E = 3,600, T = 1,080,000.
  3. u per month: static 0, yearly 1/12, quarterly 1/3, monthly 1, weekly 52/12, daily 365/12, or a number; f = change_fraction (blank = 1, full re-embed). Monthly tokens = T × u × f.
  4. Cost (quoted P only): one-time = ΣT ÷ 1M × P; monthly = Σ(T × u × f) ÷ 1M × P; first-year = one-time + 12 × monthly; round to 4 decimals; say whether monthly assumes a full re-embed or the change fraction.
  5. Retrieval budget: per-query = ceil(top_k × C ÷ r) vs context_budget_tokens; utilization %, headroom. Over budget → blocking ("top_k × chunk size = N est. tokens exceeds the context budget of B"; Fits: "NO — blocking"). With a reranker, rerank_fetch_k < top_k is blocking; unset fetch_k is a warning.
  6. Other blocking: O ≥ C; invalid corpus row. Any blocking error → verdict BLOCKED, stops (exit 1), rag-plan.json/rag-plan.md still written, no scaffold.
  7. Warnings — list every one that applies: O = 0 (zero overlap: boundary context lost); store in-memory (index lost on restart); FAISS (pickle-backed metadata); unknown store; no embedding_model; price 0; no price_date; a source with L ≤ C (fits in one chunk).
  8. Live index (current_config): changed keys over index keys (chunk_size_chars, chunk_overlap_chars, embedding_provider, embedding_model, vector_store) and query keys (top_k, reranker, rerank_fetch_k, context_budget_tokens) — a key counts only when its value differs (absent vs set counts). Any index key changed → full re-index = new total T tokens at new total T ÷ 1M × P one-off. Size both configs on the same corpus: total chunks before → after, monthly cost before → after, per-query context before → after.

Reply layout: working table first (source | D | L | n | chunks | E | T | u | f | monthly tokens), totals row, then Verdict READY/BLOCKED with exit code, then ## Sizing, ## Cost, ## Retrieval budget, [## Change vs current index as | key | current | proposed | index/query |], ## Warnings, ## Scaffold (rag_pipeline.py: config constants, one SOURCES entry per source with locations from environment variables, make_embeddings() shared by index and query, make_vector_store(), ingest(), retrieve() with optional rerank — generated and syntax-checked, not executed).

  • Required facts missing ("how much will embedding cost?"): name the run above, then ask once, in one list, for the corpus profile and the config including a dated price per 1M tokens (layouts in assets/). Do not assume a price.
  • Review requested (review=yes): after the script outputs, write rag-review.md on assets/rag-review-template.md (## Upstream conformance, ## Cost and budget risks, ## Next changes, each row with an owner) with vendor/langchain-rag/SKILL.md as context.

bodyMd:
# LangChain RAG Runner

## In a conversation: size and scaffold now
**Never**
- Never assume or "use the usual" embedding price: it has no default. A missing price → "**stops (exit 1)**: config.embedding_price_per_1m_tokens is missing (no default is assumed)"; verdict BLOCKED; no `rag_pipeline.py`. Token estimates (price-independent) may still be shown; cost is `[TO BE BASELINED — owner: ML platform lead]` with no number.
- Never replace a computable row with a TBD: every source with D and L gets n, chunks, E and T computed; only the missing value itself is a marker (a source without L shows the formula with `[TO BE BASELINED — owner: Data owner]`).
- Never call tokens exact: label them "est. tokens (characters ÷ 4, not a tokenizer count)".
- Never call the scaffold tested: `rag_pipeline.py` is "generated and syntax-checked, not executed"; code drafted in chat is a draft until that check runs.

**Every reply with corpus or config facts starts with**: "Runs `python3 -I scripts/plan_rag.py --corpus <corpus.csv> --config <rag-config.json> [--current-config <live-config.json>] --out-dir <dir>` → `rag-plan.json`, `rag-plan.md` (## Sizing, ## Cost, ## Retrieval budget, [## Change vs current index], ## Warnings, ## Scaffold) and `rag_pipeline.py` (only when not blocked)."

**Procedure (from `references/sizing-method.md` / `scripts/plan_rag.py`; compute row by row, never estimate)**
1. Required config keys: chunk_size_chars C, chunk_overlap_chars O, embedding_price_per_1m_tokens P, top_k, reranker, vector_store, context_budget_tokens; chars_per_token r = 4 unless given. Missing config or corpus file / bad JSON → **stops (exit 2)**.
2. Per source: S = C − O; n = 1 if L ≤ C else 1 + ceil((L − C) ÷ S); E = L + (n − 1) × O; chunks = D × n; T = ceil(D × E ÷ r). Check: C 1000, O 200, L 3000, D 1200 → n = 1 + ceil(2000/800) = 4, chunks 4,800, E = 3,600, T = 1,080,000.
3. u per month: static 0, yearly 1/12, quarterly 1/3, monthly 1, weekly 52/12, daily 365/12, or a number; f = change_fraction (blank = 1, full re-embed). Monthly tokens = T × u × f.
4. Cost (quoted P only): one-time = ΣT ÷ 1M × P; monthly = Σ(T × u × f) ÷ 1M × P; first-year = one-time + 12 × monthly; round to 4 decimals; say whether monthly assumes a full re-embed or the change fraction.
5. Retrieval budget: per-query = ceil(top_k × C ÷ r) vs context_budget_tokens; utilization %, headroom. Over budget → blocking ("top_k × chunk size = N est. tokens exceeds the context budget of B"; Fits: "NO — blocking"). With a reranker, rerank_fetch_k < top_k is blocking; unset fetch_k is a warning.
6. Other blocking: O ≥ C; invalid corpus row. Any blocking error → verdict BLOCKED, **stops (exit 1)**, `rag-plan.json`/`rag-plan.md` still written, no scaffold.
7. Warnings — list every one that applies: O = 0 (zero overlap: boundary context lost); store in-memory (index lost on restart); FAISS (pickle-backed metadata); unknown store; no embedding_model; price 0; no price_date; a source with L ≤ C (fits in one chunk).
8. Live index (`current_config`): changed keys over index keys (chunk_size_chars, chunk_overlap_chars, embedding_provider, embedding_model, vector_store) and query keys (top_k, reranker, rerank_fetch_k, context_budget_tokens) — a key counts only when its value differs (absent vs set counts). Any index key changed → full re-index = new total T tokens at new total T ÷ 1M × P one-off. Size both configs on the same corpus: total chunks before → after, monthly cost before → after, per-query context before → after.

**Reply layout**: working table first (source | D | L | n | chunks | E | T | u | f | monthly tokens), totals row, then Verdict READY/BLOCKED with exit code, then ## Sizing, ## Cost, ## Retrieval budget, [## Change vs current index as | key | current | proposed | index/query |], ## Warnings, ## Scaffold (`rag_pipeline.py`: config constants, one `SOURCES` entry per source with locations from environment variables, `make_embeddings()` shared by index and query, `make_vector_store()`, `ingest()`, `retrieve()` with optional rerank — generated and syntax-checked, not executed).
- **Required facts missing** ("how much will embedding cost?"): name the run above, then ask once, in one list, for the corpus profile and the config including a dated price per 1M tokens (layouts in `assets/`). Do not assume a price.
- **Review requested** (`review=yes`): after the script outputs, write `rag-review.md` on `assets/rag-review-template.md` (## Upstream conformance, ## Cost and budget risks, ## Next changes, each row with an owner) with `vendor/langchain-rag/SKILL.md` as context.

Wraps langchain-rag from langchain-ai/langchain-skills (pinned in vendor/pins.json). The upstream skill is instructions only; this skill turns its splitter, embedding and vector-store guidance into sizing and cost arithmetic, blocking config checks and a generated scaffold. Upstream text is not copied: the optional review step reads `vendor/langchain-rag/SKILL.md` directly.

## Starting points
- **New** — size, cost and scaffold a pipeline from a corpus profile and the settings you plan.
- **Existing** — also pass the config the live index was built with as `current_config`: both are sized on the same corpus and the plan adds "Change vs current index" (changed keys, whether a full re-index is needed and its one-off cost, deltas in chunks, monthly cost and context per query).

## When to use
- Before building a LangChain RAG pipeline: how many chunks, how many embedding tokens, what it costs to embed and keep fresh, whether `top_k` chunks fit the context.
- When a chunking, `top_k` or store choice changes and the cost or budget must be re-checked.
- NOT for: measuring retrieval quality or choosing between chunking strategies (`rag-pipeline-design`), serving capacity (`infra-gpu-sizing`), running evals (`llm-eval-harness`).

## Inputs required
| Input | Required | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `corpus` — one row per source: doc count, average characters, update frequency, optional change fraction | yes | data owner; layout `assets/corpus-profile.example.csv` |
| `config` — chunk size and overlap (chars), embedding price per 1M tokens, `top_k`, reranker yes/no, vector store, context budget (tokens available for retrieved text) | yes | ML platform lead; layout `assets/rag-config.example.json` |
| optional config: embedding model and provider, `rerank_fetch_k`, chars per token (default 4), currency, price date | no | ML platform lead |
| `review` — flag for the optional LLM review | no | user |

The embedding price has no default: a missing price blocks the run. A missing model, price date or rerank candidate count becomes `[TO BE BASELINED — owner: <role>]`.

## Procedure
1. Read `../../../shared/quality-bar.md`.
2. Fill the corpus profile and config from `assets/`. Use measured averages (from a sample) rather than guesses; record the price date.
3. Run the skill. `scripts/plan_rag.py` applies `references/sizing-method.md`: chunks per document from the sliding window, embedded characters including overlap, tokens as characters ÷ chars-per-token (an estimate), one-time and monthly re-embedding cost, per-query context vs budget.
4. Blocking (exit 1): a missing required key, overlap ≥ chunk size, `rerank_fetch_k` < `top_k`, `top_k` × chunk tokens over the context budget, an invalid corpus row. Fix and re-run.
5. Read the Warnings: zero overlap, in-memory store, FAISS deserialization, missing model or price date, documents shorter than one chunk.
6. `rag_pipeline.py` holds the config constants, one `SOURCES` entry per corpus source (locations from environment variables), `make_embeddings()` (one embeddings object for index and query), `make_vector_store()` for chroma, faiss, inmemory, pinecone or pgvector, `ingest()` and `retrieve()` with optional rerank. It was generated and syntax-checked, not executed.
7. Optional: pass `review=yes` for `rag-review.md` on `assets/rag-review-template.md`.
8. Run the self-check.

## Output
| File | Content | Checks |
|---|---|---|
| `rag-plan.json` | ok flag, config, method, per-source sizing and cost, totals, retrieval budget, warnings, scaffold status | json; `"ok": true` |
| `rag-plan.md` | Sizing, Cost, Retrieval budget, Warnings, Scaffold | sections; no unowned TBD; every number traces to `rag-plan.json` |
| `rag_pipeline.py` | LangChain ingestion + retrieval scaffold | syntax check with required functions; splitter wired to config |
| `rag-review.md` (optional) | Upstream conformance, Cost and budget risks, Next changes | eval case `agent-with-review` |

## Self-check
- [ ] Every price is a dated user input; nothing assumed
- [ ] Token counts are labelled estimates (characters ÷ chars-per-token), not tokenizer counts
- [ ] Monthly cost states whether it assumes a full re-embed or a change fraction
- [ ] `top_k` × chunk fits the context budget with headroom for the prompt and answer
- [ ] Index and query use the same embeddings object; the store persists beyond tests
- [ ] `rag_pipeline.py` is described as syntax-checked, not run

## References
- `references/sizing-method.md` — formulas, a hand-checked example, and limits
- `scripts/plan_rag.py` — calculator and generator (argparse; stdlib)
- `scripts/check_syntax.py` — compile/ast check used by the output check
- `assets/corpus-profile.example.csv`, `assets/rag-config.example.json` — input layouts
- `assets/rag-review-template.md` — template for the optional review
- Upstream: `vendor/langchain-rag/SKILL.md` (langchain-ai/langchain-skills, MIT, pinned in vendor/pins.json)

## How to run (automation, when commands can run)

LangGraph HITL Runner

In a conversation: write the approval gates now

  • The request names the gated actions (e.g. finance approves refunds, a team lead approves customer emails): write the gates in this reply, in this order. (1) The approval-points spec as JSON in the assets/approvals.example.json layout — graph, checkpointer, state_fields, and per gate before_node, reason, approver_role, timeout_minutes, on_timeout (reject, escalate or auto-approve), escalate_to, editable_fields, high_impact, irreversible. Use only the roles the user named; every timeout, escalation role, editable field and checkpointer not stated is To be baselined · owner: Process owner (checkpointer: Engineering lead), and the reply asks for them once in one list. (2) The approval matrix table: gate, reason, approver role, timeout, on-timeout policy, escalation role, editable fields, high-impact, irreversible. (3) The rules that apply (references/approval-rules.md): a high-impact or irreversible gate needs a timeout; an irreversible action (money out, a sent email) never auto-approves on timeout; the memory checkpointer is development only — postgres or sqlite otherwise. (4) The resume flow: start runs to the interrupt() in approve_<node> (interrupt first — code before it re-runs on resume); the approver's decision comes back via resume with the same thread_id and Command(resume=...) only; Command(goto=...) routes to the action or to reject/escalate; side effects sit in the action node after approval and are idempotent; a scheduler calls resume_on_timeout because LangGraph has no timer; approver identity is checked in resume. (5) The hitl.py contents: GATES, the approve_<node> and escalate_<node> gates, action stubs, make_checkpointer(), build_graph(), start / resume / resume_on_timeout. Say scripts/build_hitl.py validates the spec and generates hitl.py, which is syntax-checked, not executed; code drafted in chat is a draft until that run. Then give the run command.
  • Nothing about the actions is given ("add human approval to my agent"): ask once, in one list, for each action to gate, why, the approver role, timeout and on-timeout policy, escalation role, fields the approver may edit, whether it is high-impact or irreversible, and the checkpointer. Do not invent approvers or timeouts.
  • Asked for an unsafe gate (auto-approve a payment or other irreversible action on silence, no checkpointer, no approver, a high-impact gate with no timeout): decline in one line per rule with the reason (silence must not trigger an action that cannot be undone; without a checkpointer an interrupt cannot resume), say the validation fails and no hitl.py is written, and offer the safe version: escalate or reject on timeout, a postgres checkpointer, a named approver.
  • An existing graph is given: fit each gate to a real node, list the incoming edges to rewire to each approve_<node>, and name the tool nodes left ungated for the risk owner to accept or gate.

# LangGraph HITL Runner

## In a conversation: write the approval gates now
- **The request names the gated actions** (e.g. finance approves refunds, a team lead approves customer emails): write the gates **in this reply**, in this order. (1) The approval-points spec as JSON in the `assets/approvals.example.json` layout — `graph`, `checkpointer`, `state_fields`, and per gate `before_node`, `reason`, `approver_role`, `timeout_minutes`, `on_timeout` (reject, escalate or auto-approve), `escalate_to`, `editable_fields`, `high_impact`, `irreversible`. Use only the roles the user named; every timeout, escalation role, editable field and checkpointer not stated is `[TO BE BASELINED — owner: Process owner]` (checkpointer: Engineering lead), and the reply asks for them once in one list. (2) The approval matrix table: gate, reason, approver role, timeout, on-timeout policy, escalation role, editable fields, high-impact, irreversible. (3) The rules that apply (`references/approval-rules.md`): a high-impact or irreversible gate needs a timeout; an irreversible action (money out, a sent email) never auto-approves on timeout; the memory checkpointer is development only — postgres or sqlite otherwise. (4) The resume flow: `start` runs to the `interrupt()` in `approve_<node>` (interrupt first — code before it re-runs on resume); the approver's decision comes back via `resume` with the **same `thread_id`** and `Command(resume=...)` only; `Command(goto=...)` routes to the action or to reject/escalate; side effects sit in the action node after approval and are idempotent; a scheduler calls `resume_on_timeout` because LangGraph has no timer; approver identity is checked in `resume`. (5) The `hitl.py` contents: `GATES`, the `approve_<node>` and `escalate_<node>` gates, action stubs, `make_checkpointer()`, `build_graph()`, `start` / `resume` / `resume_on_timeout`. Say `scripts/build_hitl.py` validates the spec and generates `hitl.py`, which is syntax-checked, not executed; code drafted in chat is a draft until that run. Then give the run command.
- **Nothing about the actions is given** ("add human approval to my agent"): ask once, in one list, for each action to gate, why, the approver role, timeout and on-timeout policy, escalation role, fields the approver may edit, whether it is high-impact or irreversible, and the checkpointer. Do not invent approvers or timeouts.
- **Asked for an unsafe gate** (auto-approve a payment or other irreversible action on silence, no checkpointer, no approver, a high-impact gate with no timeout): decline in one line per rule with the reason (silence must not trigger an action that cannot be undone; without a checkpointer an interrupt cannot resume), say the validation fails and no `hitl.py` is written, and offer the safe version: escalate or reject on timeout, a postgres checkpointer, a named approver.
- **An existing graph is given**: fit each gate to a real node, list the incoming edges to rewire to each `approve_<node>`, and name the tool nodes left ungated for the risk owner to accept or gate.

bodyHtml:
LangGraph Runner

Wraps langgraph-fundamentals from langchain-ai/langchain-skills (pinned in vendor/pins.json). The upstream skill is instructions only; this skill turns its graph rules into deterministic checks and a generated scaffold. Upstream text is not copied here: the optional review step reads vendor/langgraph-fundamentals/SKILL.md and its Python reference directly.

In a conversation: validate the graph now

Never

  • Never invent nodes, state fields or routes: anything absent from the spec is an error, not a guess.
  • Never write or show a graph.py scaffold for a spec with any error: the run stops (exit 1), validation.json and graph.md are still written and graph.md says "No scaffold was written".
  • Never call the scaffold tested or working: it is "generated and syntax-checked (compile() + ast.parse), not executed" — langgraph is not imported.
  • Never rename the outputs: validation.json, graph.md, graph.py, and (review only) graph-review.md.

Every reply that has or refers to a spec — including "here is my spec" with the file not shown — starts with these lines (copy them):

  1. "Runs python3 -I scripts/build_graph.py --spec <spec.json> [--current-spec <live-spec.json>] --out-dir <dir>."
  2. "validation.json reports valid (true/false), the errors and the warnings."
  3. "graph.md shows the Mermaid diagram (## Diagram), the validation table (## Validation), the node table plus state table (## Nodes) and how to run (## How to run)."
  4. "graph.py (StateGraph scaffold) is generated and syntax-checked, not executed; it is written only when the spec is valid."

If the spec's content is not in the conversation, follow those lines with the expected section skeletons and ask once for the spec per assets/graph-spec.example.json; never stop at only a request.

Procedure (rules from references/graph-validation-rules.md / scripts/build_graph.py; check node by node from the supplied spec)

  1. Graph = spec nodes + START + END; edges = START → entry, each static edge, each finish node → END, each conditional route from -[label]-> to.
  2. Errors (exit 1): spec shape (name, state, nodes, entry); node names unique Python identifiers, not START/END/State/build_graph; kind in llm|tool|router|function; field type in str/int/float/bool/list/dict/any/messages, reducer add or add_messages compatible with the type; dangling edge (from/to not a node or END); any edge or route into START; node not reachable from entry; END not reachable from a node; a cycle (SCC of size > 1 or self-loop) with no conditional edge leaving it ("has no conditional exit"); a router with < 2 routes; two conditional blocks from one node; a reads/writes entry that is not a declared field ("undeclared state field 'x'").
  3. Warnings (exit 0): a node with static AND conditional out-edges; a list field written by ≥ 2 nodes without a reducer; a declared field nobody reads or writes; a node without a description.
  4. Missing or non-JSON spec → stops (exit 2) and asks for it.

Reply layout: a working table first (rule → nodes/fields checked → pass/error/warning), then valid: true|false with exit code, then graph.md (Diagram as a mermaid flowchart, Validation, Nodes + state, How to run), then the graph.py shape (TypedDict State with Annotated reducers, one stub per node, one route_<node> per conditional block returning a Literal of its labels, add_node/add_edge/add_conditional_edges wiring, builder.compile(...)) with the syntax-checked-not-executed statement.

  • Invalid spec: list each error with its fix; say "stops (exit 1); no graph.py written".
  • Review requested (review=yes): after the script outputs, write graph-review.md on assets/graph-review-template.md — Bottom line, ## Upstream conformance (the six area rows, citing the upstream vendor/langgraph-fundamentals/SKILL.md and its Python reference as the source), ## Design risks (each with an owner), ## Next changes (each with an owner) — and say the upstream langgraph-fundamentals skill is its context.
  • Current spec given (current_spec): add "## Changes vs current graph" — nodes added/removed/kind changed, edges (as from, to, route label over the edge set above) added/removed, state fields added/removed/changed (type/reducer -> type/reducer); total_changes = nodes + edges + state (+1 if entry changed). A removed field or a changed type or reducer is listed in resume_breaking_fields: threads checkpointed under the current graph cannot resume safely.

Starting points

  • New — validate a graph spec written from assets/graph-spec.example.json and generate the StateGraph scaffold.
  • Existing — also pass the spec of the graph running today as current_spec: graph.md adds "Changes vs current graph" (nodes, edges/routes and state fields added, removed or changed) and flags state changes that break resuming threads already checkpointed.

When to use

  • A LangGraph workflow has been sketched (nodes, state, routing) and needs checking before code is written.
  • An existing graph spec changed and must be re-validated (orphans, infinite loops, dangling routes).
  • NOT for: deciding whether to build an agent at all (agent-architecture), adding approval interrupts (langgraph-hitl-runner), retrieval design (langchain-rag-runner), running evals (llm-eval-harness).

Inputs required

InputRequiredSource

review — flag for the optional LLM review against upstream guidancenouser

Nothing is inferred: a node, field, or route absent from the spec is an error, not a guess. Field types: str, int, float, bool, list, dict, any, messages. Reducers: add (operator.add) or add_messages.

Procedure

  1. Read ../../../shared/quality-bar.md.
  2. Fill the spec from assets/graph-spec.example.json. One node per discrete step; classify each as llm, tool, router or function; declare every state field each node reads or writes.
  3. Run the skill. scripts/build_graph.py applies the rules in references/graph-validation-rules.md: reachability from entry, END reachable from every node, a conditional exit on every cycle, no dangling edges, routers with at least two routes, START used only as the entry, declared state references, reducer warnings for multi-writer list fields, static-plus-conditional warnings.
  4. On exit 1, read the Errors list in graph.md (or validation.json), fix the spec, re-run. No graph.py is written for an invalid spec.
  5. On exit 0, graph.py holds a TypedDict state, one stub per node, one route_<node> function per conditional block, the edge wiring and compile(). It was generated and syntax-checked (compile() + ast.parse), not executed: langgraph is not imported at check time.
  6. Optional: pass review=yes for graph-review.md, an LLM review on assets/graph-review-template.md using the upstream skill and the run outputs as context.
  7. Run the self-check.

bodyMd:
# LangGraph Runner

Wraps langgraph-fundamentals from langchain-ai/langchain-skills (pinned in vendor/pins.json). The upstream skill is instructions only; this skill turns its graph rules into deterministic checks and a generated scaffold. Upstream text is not copied here: the optional review step reads `vendor/langgraph-fundamentals/SKILL.md` and its Python reference directly.

## In a conversation: validate the graph now
**Never**
- Never invent nodes, state fields or routes: anything absent from the spec is an error, not a guess.
- Never write or show a `graph.py` scaffold for a spec with any error: the run **stops (exit 1)**, `validation.json` and `graph.md` are still written and `graph.md` says "No scaffold was written".
- Never call the scaffold tested or working: it is "generated and syntax-checked (`compile()` + `ast.parse`), not executed" — langgraph is not imported.
- Never rename the outputs: `validation.json`, `graph.md`, `graph.py`, and (review only) `graph-review.md`.

**Every reply that has or refers to a spec — including "here is my spec" with the file not shown — starts with these lines (copy them):**
1. "Runs `python3 -I scripts/build_graph.py --spec <spec.json> [--current-spec <live-spec.json>] --out-dir <dir>`."
2. "`validation.json` reports `valid` (true/false), the errors and the warnings."
3. "`graph.md` shows the Mermaid diagram (## Diagram), the validation table (## Validation), the node table plus state table (## Nodes) and how to run (## How to run)."
4. "`graph.py` (StateGraph scaffold) is generated and syntax-checked, not executed; it is written only when the spec is valid."
If the spec's content is not in the conversation, follow those lines with the expected section skeletons and ask once for the spec per `assets/graph-spec.example.json`; never stop at only a request.

**Procedure (rules from `references/graph-validation-rules.md` / `scripts/build_graph.py`; check node by node from the supplied spec)**
1. Graph = spec nodes + START + END; edges = START → entry, each static edge, each finish node → END, each conditional route `from -[label]-> to`.
2. Errors (exit 1): spec shape (name, state, nodes, entry); node names unique Python identifiers, not START/END/`State`/`build_graph`; kind in llm|tool|router|function; field type in str/int/float/bool/list/dict/any/messages, reducer `add` or `add_messages` compatible with the type; dangling edge (from/to not a node or END); any edge or route into START; node not reachable from entry; END not reachable from a node; a cycle (SCC of size > 1 or self-loop) with no conditional edge leaving it ("has no conditional exit"); a `router` with < 2 routes; two conditional blocks from one node; a reads/writes entry that is not a declared field ("undeclared state field 'x'").
3. Warnings (exit 0): a node with static AND conditional out-edges; a list field written by ≥ 2 nodes without a reducer; a declared field nobody reads or writes; a node without a description.
4. Missing or non-JSON spec → **stops (exit 2)** and asks for it.

**Reply layout**: a working table first (rule → nodes/fields checked → pass/error/warning), then `valid: true|false` with exit code, then graph.md (Diagram as a mermaid flowchart, Validation, Nodes + state, How to run), then the graph.py shape (TypedDict `State` with `Annotated` reducers, one stub per node, one `route_<node>` per conditional block returning a `Literal` of its labels, `add_node`/`add_edge`/`add_conditional_edges` wiring, `builder.compile(...)`) with the syntax-checked-not-executed statement.
- **Invalid spec**: list each error with its fix; say "stops (exit 1); no graph.py written".
- **Review requested** (`review=yes`): after the script outputs, write `graph-review.md` on `assets/graph-review-template.md` — Bottom line, **## Upstream conformance** (the six area rows, citing the upstream `vendor/langgraph-fundamentals/SKILL.md` and its Python reference as the source), **## Design risks** (each with an owner), **## Next changes** (each with an owner) — and say the upstream langgraph-fundamentals skill is its context.
- **Current spec given** (`current_spec`): add "## Changes vs current graph" — nodes added/removed/kind changed, edges (as from, to, route label over the edge set above) added/removed, state fields added/removed/changed (`type/reducer -> type/reducer`); total_changes = nodes + edges + state (+1 if entry changed). A removed field or a changed type or reducer is listed in `resume_breaking_fields`: threads checkpointed under the current graph cannot resume safely.

## Starting points
- **New** — validate a graph spec written from `assets/graph-spec.example.json` and generate the StateGraph scaffold.
- **Existing** — also pass the spec of the graph running today as `current_spec`: graph.md adds "Changes vs current graph" (nodes, edges/routes and state fields added, removed or changed) and flags state changes that break resuming threads already checkpointed.

## When to use
- A LangGraph workflow has been sketched (nodes, state, routing) and needs checking before code is written.
- An existing graph spec changed and must be re-validated (orphans, infinite loops, dangling routes).
- NOT for: deciding whether to build an agent at all (`agent-architecture`), adding approval interrupts (`langgraph-hitl-runner`), retrieval design (`langchain-rag-runner`), running evals (`llm-eval-harness`).

## Inputs required
| Input | Required | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `spec` — graph spec JSON (state fields with type and reducer; nodes with kind, description, reads, writes; static and conditional edges; entry; finish nodes) | yes | user / architect; layout `assets/graph-spec.example.json` |
| `review` — flag for the optional LLM review against upstream guidance | no | user |

Nothing is inferred: a node, field, or route absent from the spec is an error, not a guess. Field types: str, int, float, bool, list, dict, any, messages. Reducers: `add` (operator.add) or `add_messages`.

## Procedure
1. Read `../../../shared/quality-bar.md`.
2. Fill the spec from `assets/graph-spec.example.json`. One node per discrete step; classify each as llm, tool, router or function; declare every state field each node reads or writes.
3. Run the skill. `scripts/build_graph.py` applies the rules in `references/graph-validation-rules.md`: reachability from entry, END reachable from every node, a conditional exit on every cycle, no dangling edges, routers with at least two routes, START used only as the entry, declared state references, reducer warnings for multi-writer list fields, static-plus-conditional warnings.
4. On exit 1, read the Errors list in `graph.md` (or `validation.json`), fix the spec, re-run. No `graph.py` is written for an invalid spec.
5. On exit 0, `graph.py` holds a TypedDict state, one stub per node, one `route_<node>` function per conditional block, the edge wiring and `compile()`. It was generated and syntax-checked (`compile()` + `ast.parse`), not executed: langgraph is not imported at check time.
6. Optional: pass `review=yes` for `graph-review.md`, an LLM review on `assets/graph-review-template.md` using the upstream skill and the run outputs as context.
7. Run the self-check.

## Output
| File | Content | Checks |
|---|---|---|
| `validation.json` | valid flag, errors, warnings, stats, unreachable nodes, nodes with no path to END, cycles with their conditional exits, scaffold status | json; `"valid": true` |
| `graph.md` | Diagram (Mermaid), Validation, Nodes (+ state table), How to run | sections; mermaid parses; no unowned TBD |
| `graph.py` | StateGraph scaffold | syntax check via `scripts/check_syntax.py`; contains `builder.compile(` |
| `graph-review.md` (optional) | Upstream conformance, Design risks, Next changes | eval case `agent-with-review` |

## Self-check
- [ ] `validation.json` says `"valid": true`, and every warning is accepted or fixed
- [ ] Every loop has a conditional exit; END is reachable from every node
- [ ] List fields written by several nodes carry a reducer
- [ ] No node has both static and conditional out-edges unless both branches are meant to run
- [ ] `graph.md` states the scaffold was syntax-checked, not executed
- [ ] Stubs were implemented and the graph was run in a langgraph environment before anyone calls it working

## References
- `references/graph-validation-rules.md` — each rule, why it exists, and how it is computed
- `scripts/build_graph.py` — validator and generator (argparse; stdlib)
- `scripts/check_syntax.py` — compile/ast check used by the output check
- `assets/graph-spec.example.json` — spec layout to copy
- `assets/graph-review-template.md` — template for the optional review
- Upstream: `vendor/langgraph-fundamentals/SKILL.md` (langchain-ai/langchain-skills, MIT, pinned in vendor/pins.json)

## How to run (automation, when commands can run)
This skill is executable. Collect the inputs below, then run `python3 scripts/run_skill.py ai-platform/langgraph-runner --input <name>=<value> … --out <dir>` (see `--explain ai-platform/langgraph-runner`). Report the `run.json` results; do not hand-write the deliverables the scripts produce (`graph.py`, `graph.md`, `validation.json`). A failed validation (exit 1) is the gate working: fix the spec and re-run.

How to run

This skill is executable. Collect the inputs below, then run python3 scripts/run_skill.py ai-platform/llm-eval-harness --input <name>=<value> … --out <dir> (see --explain ai-platform/llm-eval-harness). Report the run.json results; do not hand-write the deliverables the scripts produce.

Starting points

  • New — turn raw cases or a transcript into a golden set and run the regression gate on recorded outputs.
  • Existing — pass your current golden set as existing_golden (with the candidate's outputs in an output column), new production cases as cases, and last release's scorecard as baseline (optionally max_regression): the set is extended without renumbering (golden-merge.json) and the scorecard adds a per-case comparison (newly failing, newly passing, new cases).

When to use

  • Before first release of any LLM feature or agent; before every prompt/model/tool change thereafter.
  • Answering "is it good enough" with numbers instead of demos.
  • NOT for: retrieval tuning alone (rag-pipeline-design), load testing, security pen-testing.

Inputs required

InputRequiredSource
The system under test: how to call it (function, HTTP endpoint, CLI) and its input/output shapeyesuser / repo
What "good" means: the task definition and the failure types the owner fears mostyesuser
Real examples: ≥ 30 inputs with expected outputs or acceptance notesyesuser / logs; if absent, ask — synthetic cases are labeled and capped at 30% of the set
Risk tier (internal / employee-facing / customer-facing / regulated)yesuser
Release cadence and CI systemnorepo

If the system interface or the real examples are missing, ask once.

Procedure

  1. Read ../../../shared/quality-bar.md and ../../../shared/token-efficiency.md.
  2. Build the golden set with references/golden-set.md into assets/golden-set.csv: id, input, expected (or acceptance keywords/regex), category, difficulty, must-not-contain, source, weight.
  3. Design the rubric with references/rubric-design.md into assets/eval-rubric.csv: criterion, definition, scale, pass threshold, scoring method (deterministic / judge / human), weight.
  4. Wire the runner. Copy scripts/run_evals.py; implement call_system(input) -> output for the system under test. Default scoring is deterministic (keywords, regex, must-not-contain, exact match, JSON validity). Add an LLM judge only for criteria that cannot be scored deterministically, following references/llm-as-judge.md.
  5. Run baseline. python3 -I scripts/run_evals.py --golden assets/golden-set.csv --rubric assets/eval-rubric.csv --out scorecard.json. Record the baseline per category.
  6. Set the gate with references/regression-gating.md: overall threshold, per-category minimums, zero-tolerance checks (safety, must-not-contain), and max regression vs baseline. Add the runner to CI (pytest collects it).
  7. Report the scorecard: table by category, failures with ids, gate result, recommended fixes.
  8. Run the self-check.

Output

  • assets/golden-set.csv, assets/eval-rubric.csv filled; scripts/run_evals.py adapted; scorecard.json; CI job snippet.
  • Scorecard table in the reply: category | n | pass rate | mean score | gate.

Self-check

  • [ ] ≥ 30 cases; synthetic share ≤ 30% and labeled
  • [ ] Every rubric criterion has a scoring method and threshold
  • [ ] Deterministic checks used wherever possible; judge only where needed, with calibration plan
  • [ ] Zero-tolerance checks defined for the risk tier
  • [ ] Gate fails the build on threshold or regression breach
  • [ ] Baseline recorded with model/prompt version
  • [ ] No quality claims without the scorecard

References

  • references/golden-set.md — construction, coverage, sourcing, maintenance
  • references/rubric-design.md — criteria, scales, thresholds, weights
  • references/llm-as-judge.md — pitfalls and controls
  • references/regression-gating.md — thresholds, CI wiring, drift monitoring
  • scripts/run_evals.py — runner (pytest-compatible)

If the system interface or the real examples are missing, ask once.

card: Dashboard and alerts from your LLM traces
name: llm-observability
description: Use when an LLM feature is live and the user needs to know how it is behaving from its traces — "monitor our LLM traces", "set up LLM monitoring", "are we meeting our SLOs", "check the last 24h p95 for a feature", "p95 latency and cost per request by feature", "has quality drifted since last week", "what should our trace schema be". Produces dashboard.json and alerts.md (Status, SLO breaches, Drift, By feature) from trace spans (JSONL) and the owner's SLO CSV - request count, error rate, nearest-rank p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens and cost per request (only from spans that carry cost_usd, never estimated from token prices), eval score mean, drift against a baseline window - plus the recommended trace schema. Never picks SLO thresholds. Not for app logging/Sentry setup (observability-setup), offline evals (llm-eval-harness), incident handling (ai-incident-runbook), SLO design from a request log (ai-slo-definition) or team spend showback (ai-finops-chargeback).

inputs.name: traces
inputs.from: trace spans as JSONL, one span per line (schema: assets/trace-schema.json)

inputs.name: slo
inputs.from: SLO rows metric,threshold,window[,feature][,comparator] (layout: assets/slo-template.csv); owner-supplied

inputs.name: baseline_start
inputs.from: baseline window start date, e.g. 2026-09-01 (drift needs both baseline dates)

inputs.name: baseline_end
inputs.from: baseline window end date (inclusive)

existing.bring: trace exports from your running app and your SLO targets

bodyHtml:
LLM Observability (traces → SLOs → alerts)

In a conversation: set up the roll-up now

The reply gives the monitoring setup and the exact inputs it needs; numbers appear only from real spans.

  • The feature is live but traces and SLOs are not in the conversation ("are we meeting SLOs, has latency drifted", or files said to be attached): in this reply give
    1. What to send: the trace export as JSONL and the SLO thresholds from the service owner. Never propose thresholds as the SLO; show the SLO CSV skeleton (metric,threshold,window,feature,comparator, rows for error_rate, latency_p95_ms, eval_score_mean, cost_per_request_usd, drift_*_pct) with each threshold To be baselined · owner: service owner.
    2. Trace fields per assets/trace-schema.json: required trace_id, ts, feature, model, latency_ms, input_tokens, output_tokens, status; optional cost_usd, eval_score, user_feedback. Spans missing required fields are rejected and counted, never repaired. Cost per request is reported only from spans that carry cost_usd, with coverage; without it the cost SLO reads NO DATA.
    3. Drift: against a baseline window once both dates are given (convert "first week of September" to baseline_start/baseline_end and confirm the year); drift = (current − baseline) ÷ baseline × 100 for tokens per request, p95 latency and eval score mean.
    4. The run: python3 -I scripts/observe.py --traces spans.jsonl --slo slo.csv --out-dir <dir> [--baseline-start …] [--baseline-end …] → dashboard.json, alerts.md (Status, SLO breaches, Drift, By feature), trace-schema.json; percentiles nearest-rank; any BREACH exits 1. Do not print metric values that were not computed.
  • Asked to pick sensible SLOs: decline in one line (a threshold is the service owner's commitment, not this skill's); show the skeleton with markers and ask for the values.
  • Asked to estimate cost from token prices (cost not logged): decline in one line; the cost SLO for that feature is NO DATA, reported and never counted as met; the fix is to instrument cost_usd on spans. Still report the other SLOs, e.g. a p95 above its threshold in its window is a BREACH and exits 1.
  • Nothing about the app: ask once for the feature names, the trace source (OpenTelemetry, Langfuse, provider logs) and the SLO owner.

Starting points

  • Existing — rolls up spans your running application already emitted against the owner's SLOs, with drift against a baseline window.
  • Only for existing: there is nothing to measure until an application produces traces; for a new app, emit spans per assets/trace-schema.json and set SLOs from assets/slo-template.csv, then run this on the first traffic.

When to use

  • A deployed LLM/agent feature needs per-feature latency, error, token, cost and quality roll-ups against SLOs.
  • "Has it drifted?" — compare the current window to a baseline window.
  • Defining what every span must log (trace schema) before go-live.
  • NOT for: application logging, Sentry or health checks (observability-setup), building eval sets (llm-eval-harness), running an incident (ai-incident-runbook), release gates (ai-release-plan).

Inputs required

InputRequiredSource
traces JSONL: trace_id, ts, feature/route, model, latency_ms, input_tokens, output_tokens, status; optional cost_usd, eval_score, user_feedbackyestracing export (OpenTelemetry, Langfuse, provider logs) mapped to assets/trace-schema.json
slo CSV: metric, threshold, window, optional feature and comparatoryesservice owner; the skill never sets a threshold
baseline_start, baseline_endnoowner; without them drift is not computed

If traces or slo is missing the runner exits 2 and asks once. Spans missing required fields are rejected and counted, never repaired.

Procedure

  1. Read ../../../shared/quality-bar.md.
  2. Map the trace export to assets/trace-schema.json (the script copies it to the output as the reference schema).
  3. Fill assets/slo-template.csv with the owner's thresholds and windows.
  4. Run the skill. The script splits baseline/current windows, computes the metrics in references/metrics-method.md per feature and overall, and evaluates each SLO in its window.
  5. Read alerts.md: Status first, then breaches, then drift and the feature table.
  6. NO DATA rows mean the signal is not instrumented (e.g. no cost_usd) — instrument it; do not estimate it.
  7. Run the self-check.

Output

  • dashboard.json: windows, overall and per-feature metrics, baseline, drift, SLO results, rejected-span reasons.
  • alerts.md: Status, SLO breaches (every SLO with observed value and status), Drift, By feature.
  • trace-schema.json: the recommended span schema (JSON Schema).

Self-check

  • [ ] Percentiles are nearest-rank and labelled as such
  • [ ] Cost per request only from cost_usd on spans, with coverage shown; never from guessed prices
  • [ ] Every SLO threshold came from the SLO file; NO DATA is not reported as met
  • [ ] Drift states both windows and is relative to the baseline
  • [ ] Rejected spans counted with reasons
  • [ ] Exit 1 when any SLO is breached

References

  • references/metrics-method.md — windows, metric definitions, percentile method, drift, SLO evaluation
  • assets/trace-schema.json — recommended span schema
  • assets/slo-template.csv — SLO input layout
  • scripts/observe.py — the roll-up (argparse; stdlib)

How to run (automation, when commands can run)

This skill is executable. Collect the inputs below, then run python3 scripts/run_skill.py ai-platform/llm-observability --input <name>=<value> … --out <dir> (see --explain ai-platform/llm-observability). Report the run.json results; do not hand-write the deliverables the script produces (dashboard.json, alerts.md, trace-schema.json). Any SLO breach fails the run (exit 1) on purpose; the outputs are still written.

cases.prompt: Our claims summariser is live. Are we meeting SLOs, and has latency drifted since the first week of September? I can export traces as JSONL.
expected: Asks for the traces export and the SLO thresholds; does not propose its own thresholds as the SLO
Explains the trace fields needed (assets/trace-schema.json) and that cost is only reported when spans carry cost_usd
Offers drift against a baseline window once both dates are given

cases.prompt: Roll up the attached traces against our SLOs; baseline is 1-7 September.
expected: Runs scripts/observe.py; 20 current spans, 0 breaches; claims-summary p95 2100 ms, drift +31.25 %

cases.prompt: Monitor our LLM traces; pick sensible SLOs.
expected: Asks for the SLO file instead of inventing thresholds

cases.prompt: Check the last 24h p95 for claims-summary and the cost per request for policy-qa (we don't log cost there - just estimate it from token prices).
expected: Reports the 24h p95 breach (2100 ms > 1800) and exits 1
Cost SLO for policy-qa is NO DATA; no cost estimated from prices
p95 latency 3100 ms by nearest rank (rank ceil(0.95 × 8) = 8) — BREACH against 2000
error_rate 1/8 = 0.125 — BREACH against 0.1
Status BREACH (2 of 2 SLOs) and says the run exits 1; p50 800 ms
Labels percentiles as nearest-rank and reports cost per request as not available because no span carries cost_usd
Drift = (current − baseline) ÷ baseline × 100: tokens per request 600 → 900 = +50%, p95 latency 1100 → 1500 ms = +36.36%, eval score mean 0.85 → 0.79 = −7.06%
eval_score_mean 0.79 BREACH (comparator >= 0.8) and drift_tokens_per_request_pct 50 BREACH against 30
States both windows (baseline 1–3 Oct, current 10–12 Oct) and that any breach exits 1
Rejects span c6 for missing latency_ms and counts it (1 rejected span), without repairing it
Cost per request 0.005 USD from the 3 spans that carry cost_usd, with cost coverage 0.6 (3 of 5) — OK against 0.006
latency_p95_ms 1600 (nearest rank 5 of 5) — BREACH against 1500; run exits 1

cases.prompt: We go live with the contract-summary feature in two weeks. What exactly should every span log so you can monitor it later?
expected: Lists the required fields trace_id, ts, feature, model, latency_ms, input_tokens, output_tokens, status and the optional cost_usd, eval_score, user_feedback per assets/trace-schema.json
Says spans missing required fields will be rejected and counted, never repaired
Says cost is reported only from spans carrying cost_usd, so it must be instrumented, and SLO thresholds come from the service owner via assets/slo-template.csv

cases.prompt: Our traces are in Langfuse with OpenTelemetry gen_ai attributes (gen_ai.usage.input_tokens etc.). How do I get them into your roll-up?
expected: Explains mapping the export to the trace schema fields (e.g. input/output token attributes → input_tokens/output_tokens, duration → latency_ms, route → feature) as JSONL, one span per line
Asks for the SLO thresholds from the service owner and does not propose its own
Names the run python3 -I scripts/observe.py --traces … --slo … --out-dir … and its outputs dashboard.json, alerts.md and trace-schema.json

cases.prompt: Practitioner question: with 20 spans in the window, which latency do you report as p95, and do you interpolate?
expected: Nearest-rank: sort ascending and take the value at rank ceil(0.95 × 20) = 19
No interpolation; the reported value is always an observed latency, across ok and error spans

cases.prompt: Our SLO file says latency_p95_ms, 1800, 24h. The trace export covers 3 days and the last span is from yesterday afternoon. Which spans does the 24h SLO look at?
